key_terms.meaning: A family of random variables {X(t) : t ∈ T} on one probability space; the experiment fixes the whole function, not just one number.
The single record x(t) produced by one run of the experiment; also called a realisation.
The whole collection of possible sample functions, with a probability law on it.
State set may be discrete or continuous; index set T may be discrete (sequences) or continuous (signals).
For every n, τ and t₁…tₙ, the joint CDF of (X(t₁+τ)…X(tₙ+τ)) equals that of (X(t₁)…X(tₙ)).
E[X(t)] = μ is constant and R_X(t₁,t₂) = R_X(t₂ − t₁) depends only on the lag τ.
Time averages over one sample function equal ensemble averages; a single long record is enough.
⟨x⟩ = lim(T→∞) (1/2T)∫ from −T to T of x(t) dt, the average along one record.
Counting process with independent stationary increments where P(N(t)=n) = e^(−λt)(λt)ⁿ/n!, λ = mean arrivals per unit time.
Time between two successive arrivals; for a Poisson process the times are i.i.d. exponential with mean 1/λ.
Counts arrivals whose interarrival times are i.i.d. with any distribution F; the Poisson process is the exponential special case.
P(Xₙ₊₁ = j | Xₙ = i, Xₙ₋₁, …) = P(Xₙ₊₁ = j | Xₙ = i): the future depends on the present only.
Matrix with pᵢⱼ = P(Xₙ₊₁ = j | Xₙ = i); rows sum to 1 and the n-step matrix is Pⁿ.
State i with Σₙ pᵢᵢ⁽ⁿ⁾ = ∞, so return is certain; otherwise the state is transient.
All states communicate (irreducible) and returns occur at irregular times, with common period d = 1 (aperiodic).
Probability vector with π = πP and πⱼ ≥ 0, Σπⱼ = 1; the chain stays in it once started there.
The vector lim(n→∞) pᵢⱼ⁽ⁿ⁾, existing for all i when the chain is irreducible and aperiodic.
For a continuous-time chain, qᵢⱼ (i ≠ j) is the jump rate i → j and qᵢᵢ = −Σⱼ≠ᵢ qᵢⱼ; rows sum to 0.
Fourier transform of R_X(τ); gives the distribution of average power over frequency, in W/Hz.
For WSS input to an LTI system: S_Y(ω) = |H(ω)|² S_X(ω) and μ_Y = H(0)μ_X.
A process whose every finite set of samples is jointly normal; the mean function and covariance function fix it completely.
Zero-mean WSS process with R_X(τ) = (N₀/2)δ(τ), so S_X(ω) = N₀/2 is flat for all ω.

takeaways: A random process is one probability space plus a rule that turns each outcome into a whole time function.
Stationarity is about invariance under a time shift; ergodicity is about replacing an ensemble average by a time average.
The Poisson process is the renewal process with exponential interarrivals, and it is the only memoryless one.
The Markov property cuts history down to the present state, so P and its powers carry all the probability information.
For an irreducible aperiodic chain the limiting distribution exists, is unique, and equals the stationary distribution.
In continuous time, exponential sojourn times plus a jump chain give the generator matrix Q, and πQ = 0 replaces π = πP.
The pair R_X(τ) and S_X(ω) are a Fourier pair, so autocorrelation in time and power spread in frequency say the same thing.
An LTI system scales each frequency by |H(ω)|², so it shifts a random signal's mean but never creates new frequencies.
A Gaussian process is fully fixed by its mean and covariance functions, which makes it the standard model for noise.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine crisp definitions, one clean derivation (Poisson pmf, Chapman–Kolmogorov, or π = πP), and a worked numerical example on a small matrix or a simple RC-type system.

bank.q: Define a random process and a sample function. Classify random processes by the nature of the index set and the state space, giving one practical example of each of the four types.
outline: Definition as a family of random variables on one probability space
Sample function as one outcome, ensemble as the collection
Discrete time / continuous time versus discrete state / continuous state
Examples: coin tosses, daily closing Nifty value, thermal noise voltage, number of calls in a call centre

bank.q: Distinguish between strict-sense and wide-sense stationarity. Show that a strict-sense stationary process with finite second moment is wide-sense stationary, and explain why the converse fails.
outline: SSS: all joint CDFs invariant under time shift
WSS: constant mean, autocorrelation depends on lag only
SSS with finite second moment gives shift-invariant mean and autocorrelation, hence WSS
Converse fails: WSS fixes only first and second moments, higher-order distributions may change
Example of a WSS but not SSS process, e.g. a process with a random phase plus non-Gaussian amplitude

bank.q: State the defining postulates of a Poisson process and derive P(N(t) = n) = e^(−λt)(λt)ⁿ/n! from them. Give the mean and variance of N(t).
outline: Independent and stationary increments, N(0) = 0, no simultaneous arrivals
Increment over Δt is Bernoulli with probability λΔt + o(Δt)
Split (0,t) into n subintervals and take the limit
Mean = λt, variance = λt
Exponential interarrival times follow from the lack-of-memory argument

bank.q: State the Markov property and the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations. Explain how the n-step transition matrix is obtained from the one-step matrix.
outline: Conditional independence of future from past given present
Homogeneous chain and definition of pᵢⱼ
Chapman–Kolmogorov: pᵢⱼ⁽ᵐ⁺ⁿ⁾ = Σₖ pᵢₖ⁽ᵐ⁾ pₖⱼ⁽ⁿ⁾
Matrix form P⁽ⁿ⁾ = Pⁿ
Numerical example with a 2×2 P

bank.q: A two-state chain has P = [[0.7, 0.3], [0.4, 0.6]]. Find P², the probability of being in state 2 after three steps given that the chain starts in state 1, and classify both states.
outline: Square P correctly
Use the initial row vector e₁ and read the second component of e₁P³
Both states communicate, so irreducible
p₁₁ > 0 and p₂₂ > 0 so aperiodic
Finite irreducible chain means both states are positive recurrent

bank.q: For the transition matrix P = [[0.5, 0.5, 0], [0.25, 0.5, 0.25], [0, 0.5, 0.5]] find the stationary distribution by solving π = πP with Σπⱼ = 1. Interpret the answer as a long-run fraction of time.
outline: Write the three equations plus normalisation
Solve to get π = (0.25, 0.5, 0.25)
Note the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, so the stationary distribution is also the limiting one
Interpret πⱼ as long-run fraction of visits
Mention mean recurrence time 1/πⱼ

bank.q: A WSS process has autocorrelation R_X(τ) = A e^(−α|τ|) with A > 0 and α > 0. Find its mean-square value, its power spectral density, and the total average power.
outline: Mean-square value = R_X(0) = A
Fourier transform gives S_X(ω) = 2Aα/(α² + ω²)
Total power = (1/2π)∫ S_X(ω) dω = A, consistent with R_X(0)
State Wiener–Khinchin relation
Note units: A in V², S_X in V²/Hz

bank.q: White noise of power spectral density N₀/2 is passed through an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth B and gain 1. Find the output power spectral density and the output average power.
outline: |H(ω)|² = 1 for |ω| ≤ 2πB and 0 outside
S_Y(ω) = (N₀/2) inside the band, zero outside
Output power = (N₀/2)(2B) = N₀B
Mean remains zero since H(0) = 1 and input mean is zero
Comment on noise bandwidth

bank.q: Compare strict-sense stationarity, wide-sense stationarity and ergodicity. Explain, with the time-average definition, the conditions under which a WSS process is ergodic in the mean.
outline: Shift invariance of full distribution versus of first two moments
Ergodicity as equality of time and ensemble averages
Ergodic in mean requires the time average of X to converge to μ in mean square
Sufficient condition: (1/2T)∫ from −T to T of (R_X(τ) − μ²) dτ → 0 as T → ∞
Example: a process with a random constant offset is WSS but not ergodic in the mean

bank.q: Explain why an irreducible periodic chain can have a stationary distribution but no limiting distribution. Illustrate with the two-state chain that swaps states deterministically at every step.
outline: π = πP has a solution for any finite irreducible chain
Periodicity makes pᵢⱼ⁽ⁿ⁾ oscillate instead of converging
Deterministic swap example: P = [[0,1],[1,0]], π = (0.5, 0.5)
Pⁿ alternates between the identity and P
Limiting distribution exists only for irreducible aperiodic chains

bank.q: For a continuous-time Markov chain describe the role of the exponential sojourn time and the embedded jump chain. Derive the balance equation πQ = 0 and solve it for the two-state birth–death chain with birth rate λ and death rate μ.
outline: Memoryless sojourn is the only continuous waiting time that keeps the Markov property
Q has off-diagonal rates, diagonal negative row sums, rows summing to zero
Stationary: πQ = 0 with Σπ = 1
Two-state result π₀ = μ/(λ+μ), π₁ = λ/(λ+μ)
Compare with the discrete formula π = πP and mention the uniformisation view

bank.q: A server receives requests as a Poisson process of rate λ. Discuss how the model changes if the interarrival distribution is geometric, exponential or general, and judge which model is appropriate for a system in which arrivals cluster in bursts.
outline: Poisson as the exponential-interarrival renewal process
Discrete-time analogue: geometric interarrivals give a Bernoulli/Binomial counting process
General renewal: only the mean rate 1/E[X] is retained asymptotically
Bursty traffic violates the constant-rate and independent-increment assumptions
Recommend a Markov-modulated or batch arrival model, and state that the Poisson model underestimates queueing delay

bank.q: A Gaussian process is applied to a WSS input of an LTI system. Show that the output is Gaussian, find its mean and covariance, and assess why this makes Gaussian models convenient in signal and noise analysis.
outline: Linear functional of jointly Gaussian variables stays Gaussian
Output mean = H(0) times input mean
Output autocorrelation = R_X convolved with h and h(−·); output PSD = |H(ω)|² S_X(ω)
Gaussian is fixed by mean and covariance, so only two functions are needed
Caveat: real systems are not exactly Gaussian, and the model fails for impulsive noise

glossary.def: The set T of time instants at which the process is observed; discrete for sequences, continuous for signals.
The set of values the random variable X(t) can take.
R_X(t₁,t₂) = E[X(t₁)X(t₂)], the expected product of the process at two instants.
C_X(τ) = R_X(τ) − μ², the autocorrelation with the mean removed.
The time difference τ = t₂ − t₁ at which a WSS autocorrelation is evaluated.
μ_X(t) = E[X(t)], the average value of the process at time t.
A process N(t) that counts the number of events up to time t and never decreases.
Counts in disjoint time intervals are independent random variables.
The distribution of the count in an interval depends only on the interval length.
P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t); only the exponential and geometric laws have it.
m(t) = E[N(t)], the expected number of renewals up to time t.
States i and j communicate when each can be reached from the other with positive probability.
A state the chain may leave and never return to; Σₙ pᵢᵢ⁽ⁿ⁾ converges.
A recurrent state whose mean recurrence time is finite.
The greatest common divisor of the return times n with pᵢᵢ⁽ⁿ⁾ > 0.
A state with pᵢᵢ = 1, from which the chain never leaves.
The random time a continuous-time chain spends in a state before jumping; exponential with rate −qᵢᵢ.
The discrete chain of successive states visited, ignoring the waiting times.
R_XY(τ) = E[X(t)Y(t+τ)], the expected product of two different processes at a lag τ.
The power spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function of a WSS process.
The frequency response of an LTI system, equal to the Fourier transform of its impulse response.
K(s,t) = E[(X(s) − μ(s))(X(t) − μ(t))], the second central moment of a process at two instants.
A zero-mean WSS process whose autocorrelation is a delta and whose spectrum is flat.
A process whose power spectral density is concentrated around a single carrier frequency.
